It is written for a human reader.","text":"At Vardnes, Marit Solvang, forty-seven, watched the tide swallow her mussel bucket at 13:09, fifty-one minutes before the predicted high water. With the sea at her shed doorstep, she moved the outboard motor to the loft. Her barometer had stayed at 1003 all week. Three gulls perched on the breakwater above a fourth lying dead below.

Lighthouse keeper Anders Holm had left on March 2, leaving his cottage key with Marit. His logbook recorded tides arriving progressively earlier since July: four minutes, then nine, then twenty-two. Marit's grandmother Signe had kept the tide table for forty years; Marit knew this was no ordinary error. Vardnes had only 212 residents. The ferry Kittiwake passed the point at 16:40 on Tuesdays and Fridays; her brother Tomas, working in Bergen, usually called on Sundays.

Before dark, Marit entered Anders's cottage and found a handwritten tide table beneath the kitchen clock. It extended three weeks beyond his departure. Beside today's date stood 13:09. The next entry read: WHEN THE WELL TURNS SALT, LEAVE BEFORE THE BELL.

She carried a kitchen cup to the well behind the cottage. Signe had drawn drinking water there even during the summer droughts, when other wells failed. Marit lowered the bucket, hauled it up and tasted a little from the cup. Salt stung a split in her lip.

For a moment she stood holding the water in her mouth. Then she spat it out and checked her watch. 16:12. She had twenty-eight minutes to reach the ferry landing, if the Kittiwake was running today. She pocketed Anders's table without looking toward the lighthouse bell."}
